During black-start situations, this inertial support is initially absent, requiring black-start units to independently establish the system frequency and voltage. These units must quickly form a stable reference (i.e., act as grid-forming sources), often using internal control systems or stored kinetic energy, to energize the transmission lines and sequentially bring additional generators online, progressively rebuilding the system inertia and ensuring grid stability (Gracia et al. 2019). Black-start exercise Also known as an energy resilience readiness exercise, black-start exercises are real-world installation energy exercises that are designed to determine the ability of an installation’s backup power systems to start independently, transfer the load, and carry the load until energy from outside the installation is restored (DOD 2025). Critical material “Any nonfuel mineral, element, substance, or material that the U.S. Secretary of Energy determines (1) has a high risk of supply chain disruption and (2) serves an essential function in one or more energy technologies, including technologies that produce, transmit, store, and conserve energy” (DOE 2025). Energy resilience The ability to prepare for and adapt to changing conditions and recover rapidly from operational disruptions. Resilience includes the ability to withstand and recover from deliberate attacks, accidents, or naturally occurring threats or incidents (Hotchkiss and Dane 2019). Energy security Maintaining the uninterrupted availability of energy sources at an affordable price while minimizing the negative consequences from energy use, including efficiency, environmental, social, and geopolitical factors (NLR 2024d). 26 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. Term Definition Levelized cost of The levelized cost of energy, also called the levelized energy cost, is a energy cost of generating energy (usually electricity) for a particular system. It is an economic assessment of the cost of the energy-generating system, including all the costs over its lifetime: initial investment, operations and maintenance, fuel, and capital. The levelized cost of energy is used for investment planning and to compare different methods of electricity generation on a consistent basis. Marine/hydrokinetic A power source that is harnessed from the natural movement of water, energy including waves, tides, and river and ocean currents. Operational energy 10 U.S.C. 2924 defines operational energy as the “energy required for training, moving, and sustaining military forces and weapons platforms for military operations. The term includes energy used by tactical power systems and generators and weapons platforms” (10 U.S.C. 2924). Operational energy does not include the energy consumed by facilities on permanent U.S. Department of Energy installations and does not include the fuel consumed by nontactical vehicles. Optical power The technology to send and receive power wirelessly, using lasers to beaming potentially provide energy to remote installations and areas, unmanned aerial vehicles, and other applications. Point of need In distribution operations, point of need is a physical location designated by the commander at the tactical level where force employment, emplacement, or commodity consumption occurs (U.S. Joint Chiefs of Staff 2019, Joint Publication 4).
